newsitem.title: USA: NJ pension bond would leave it vulnerable - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: NJ pension bond would leave it vulnerable - Moody's.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service on Wednesday said that New Jersey's planned $2.9 billion pension bond sale would leave the state vulnerable if there were an economic downturn.
The rating agency, which was disclosing how it would evalute New Jersey's plan, also said that the proposed debt sale "would not improve the state's overall financial position."
The full text of the press release provided by Moody's follows:

As part of our examination of the State of New Jersey's proposed budget for fiscal 1998, Moody's is studying the state's proposal to issue bonds to extinguish the state pension systems' unfunded obligations.
With legislative action on the proposal still pending, this comment outlines the factors we will consider in reviewing the proposal and its implications for the state's credit standing.

The state's general obligation bonds are rated Aa1. As currently envisioned, an agency of the state would issue taxable bonds with some $2.9 billion of proceeds applied to pay, in full or in part, the unfunded accrued liability in several of the state-funded pension systems.

The proposal would also allow the state to depart from current requirements that limit the pace at which it may recognize unrealized gains in asset values; the state would instead recognize the full market value of pension system assets as of the latest valuation date.
Finally, the proposal would allow the state to reduce its normal contributions to the pension systems, to the extent made possible by "excess valuation assets," a term to be defined in statute.
As a result of the proposal's implementation, the state would be able to reduce its contributions to the pension systems by roughly $625 million over the next 15 months.
Against an otherwise stable credit backdrop, the proposal raises several issues.

The plan to borrow $2.9 billion would not improve the state's overall financial position. It merely shifts an existing liability from the pension systems to the state's long-term debt group of accounts.
It also modestly reduces the state's financial flexibility, as it replaces a relatively flexible obligation, essentially an actuarial estimate, with a more rigid debt obligation.
For the proposal to result in long-term economic benefit to the state, bond proceeds, once invested in the pension systems, will have to generate higher returns than the cost of borrowed funds.

While the pension system's portfolio of investments is likely to perform better than the yield on the taxable municipal bonds, such returns are not guaranteed. To the extent invested bond proceeds fail to return at least the interest cost of the bonds, the issuance of pension bonds would increase the total costs to the state.

Finally, the plan to reduce the state's pension fund contributions by some $625 million over the next 15 months raises questions about future budgetary balance. Earlier, the state had made some progress in adjusting its budget to the levels of spending affordable in light of reduced resources after recent multi-year tax cuts.

Given the duration -- six years -- of the current period of economic expansion, the risk of a slowdown is increasing. Also, the major adverse revenue impact of the tax cuts is already past. In this context, the need for a temporary measure of this scale to balance the fiscal 1998 spending plan raises questions about the state's ability to maintain fiscal balance in a possibly less benign future.

We recognize that New Jersey's credit standing is influenced by more than just this pension bond proposal. Among the clearly positive rating factors we will consider are the state's diverse and wealthy economic base and its record of strong financial control.

This record includes progress in recent years at restraining spending in key areas such as Medicaid, salary settlements, and employee health benefits. Also, the state has made reductions in the size of its workforce.
These positive factors are in addition to the state's pattern of prudent revenue forecasting and, together, contribute to its consistently strong ending cash balances.
The effects of the pension bond proposal will not be known for some time. Moody's will be assessing the likely impact within the framework described above.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
